1.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **On that day** to introduce a new event. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The expression **this song will be sung** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will sing this song]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he has made saving walls]

The singers are referring to complete protection by naming two major components, **walls** and **a rampart**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [walls and all their defenses]

This is the beginning of the song that the people of Judah will sing. It continues through 26:6. You may wish to mark the words of this song with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

Here the singers are speaking as if God’s act of saving his people were **walls and a rampart** that protect a city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [walls and a rampart that protect us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a city that is strong]

2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people who have faithful ways]

3.note: Here the singers are speaking as if a person’s firm resolve were something that is physically **supported** or held up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The steadfast mind]

The expression **supported** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that you support]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [at peace, at peace] or [peaceful, peaceful]

Isaiah is repeating the word **peace** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [in perfect peace]

The expression **it is entrusted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that mind trusts]

4.note: Here the singers are speaking as if Yahweh were **a rock of eternities**, that is, an eternal and immovable source of protection. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [{is} an eternal, unshakeable refuge]

The singers are using the possessive form to describe a **rock** that is characterized by **eternities**, that is, one that endures forever. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a rock that endures forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [forever and ever]

Isaiah is repeating the name of God in two forms, **Yah, Yahweh** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, only Yahweh]

5.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

5.q: כִּ֤י הֵשַׁח֙ יֹשְׁבֵ֣י מָר֔וֹם קִרְיָ֖ה נִשְׂגָּבָ֑ה יַשְׁפִּילֶ֤⁠נָּה יַשְׁפִּילָ⁠הּ֙ עַד אֶ֔רֶץ יַגִּיעֶ֖⁠נָּה עַד עָפָֽר
5.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [For he utterly brings down the dwellers of the height, the exalted city, to the dust]

Here the singers are speaking as if the pride and security of the city’s inhabitants were a physical **height** and as if the city itself were **exalted** above attack. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the proud inhabitants of the city they thought was secure]

The expression **the exalted city** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the city that people had exalted]

6.q: תִּרְמְסֶ֖⁠נָּה רָ֑גֶל רַגְלֵ֥י עָנִ֖י פַּעֲמֵ֥י דַלִּֽים
6.note: The singers are using **foot**, **feet**, and **steps** to represent the poor and needy people themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Poor and needy people trample it]

This is the end of the song that the people of Judah sing, which began in [26:1](ta:26). You may wish to mark the end of this song with a closing first-level quotation mark or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate the end of a first-level quotation.

The singers are using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the feet of those who are poor, the steps of those who are needy]

7.note: Isaiah is speaking of **the path** for the righteous as if the way righteous people live were a physical road. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The conduct of the righteous]

Isaiah is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those who are righteous]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evenness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is level]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the way of life that righteous people follow were **the course of the righteous** that Yahweh makes smooth and level. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you clear a straight path for the righteous people to live uprightly]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **course** that is characterized by **the righteous**, that is, the way of life that righteous people follow. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the course that righteous people travel]

8.note: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Here, **Indeed** emphatically affirms what follows and builds on the declaration in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Truly]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if following Yahweh’s commands were walking along **the path of your judgments**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [following your judgments]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **path** that is characterized by **your judgments**, that is, a way of life defined by Yahweh’s decisions. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the path defined by your judgments]

Here, **the soul** represents the whole person and his deepest longings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Our deepest desire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [What the soul desires]

Here, **your name** and **your remembrance** represent who Yahweh is and what he has done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for who you are and for what you have done]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and to remember you]

9.note: Here, **my soul** represents the whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I, I desire you]

Isaiah is using **my spirit within me** to represent his whole person in the act of earnestly seeking Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I myself seek you early] or [I myself earnestly seek you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to act rightly]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

10.note: Isaiah is presenting a possible condition in which the wicked person is shown favor. The ULT supplies the word **If** to mark this condition. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [If the wicked person is shown favor]

The expression **the wicked is favored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If someone shows the wicked person favor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in 26:9. Alternate translation: [to do right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uprightness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [right living]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how majestic Yahweh is]

11.note: Here, **your hand is high** represents Yahweh’s power being displayed and ready to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power is ready for you to act]
The pronoun **they** refers to the wicked people who oppose Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the wicked do not perceive {it}]

Isaiah is saying what he wants the wicked to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [May they perceive and have shame]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **zeal**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [at how zealously you care for your people]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **zeal** that is directed toward **the people**, that is, Yahweh’s passionate concern for his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for your passionate concern for your people]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s judgment against his enemies were **fire** that **will consume them**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your judgment against your enemies will destroy them]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peaceful conditions]

13.note: Isaiah is not using this possessive form **our God** to indicate that the people of Judah possess or control Yahweh. Rather Isaiah is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the people of Judah worship. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God we worship]

Here, **your name** represents Yahweh’s character and reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

Isaiah is using **remember your name** as a common expression of the culture to mean “acknowledge your authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we only remember you] or [but we acknowledge you only]

14.note: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [The reason is that]

Isaiah is using **visited** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punished.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you punished and destroyed them]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **memory** that relates to **them**, that is, what people remember about the dead rulers. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [their memory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **memory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what anyone remembered]

15.note: This clause is repeated for emphasis. See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Here “nation” represents the people. Alternate translation: [You have greatly increased the number of people in our nation]

16.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when they were suffering greatly]

Isaiah is using **visited** as a common expression of the culture to mean “sought” or “called upon.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your people sought you out]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if prayer were a liquid that could be **poured out** before Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your people prayed earnestly to you]
The term that the ULT translates as **prayer** refers to something that a person whispers, which in this context is a prayer. Alternate translation: [a whispered prayer]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **discipline**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you were disciplining them]

17.note: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Here, **thus** introduces the application of the simile about the pregnant woman to the experience of Isaiah and his people. Alternate translation: [so also]

17.q: כְּמ֤וֹ הָרָה֙ תַּקְרִ֣יב לָ⁠לֶ֔דֶת תָּחִ֥יל תִּזְעַ֖ק בַּ⁠חֲבָלֶ֑י⁠הָ כֵּ֛ן הָיִ֥ינוּ מִ⁠פָּנֶ֖י⁠ךָ יְהוָֽה
17.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a pregnant one who draws near to delivering** experiences pain and cries out, so also the people have been in similar anguish before Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Just as a pregnant woman who is about to give birth writhes and cries out in her pain, so we have been in anguish]

18.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the people’s anguish were literally that of a woman who has **been pregnant** and has **writhed** in labor. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have toiled greatly, we have been in great pain]

The point of this comparison is that just as having **birthed wind** would produce nothing, so also the people’s suffering has been futile and has not accomplished deliverance. Alternate translation: [as if our labor had produced nothing]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated the similar expression in [26:1](ta:26). Alternate translation: [a safe place]
In this context, the term **fallen** means “born.” Alternate translation: [have not been born]

19.note: The pronoun **Your** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, your ones having died]
The pronoun **my** refers to Isaiah, who identifies himself with Yahweh’s people who have died. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [our corpses]

The words translated as **Awake** and **sing joyfully** are imperatives, but they communicate a divine summons rather than a command, since they are addressed to the dead. Alternate translation: [You who dwell in the dust will awaken and sing joyfully]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the dead were **dwellers of the dust**, lying in the grave. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who lie in the dust]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s life-giving power were **dew** and as if this dew were radiant with **lights** that bring the dead back to life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your life-giving power revives the dead]

Isaiah is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could give birth to the dead. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the dead will rise from the earth]

20.note: The implied “you” in the imperative **hide** is feminine singular, even though the terms **your** and **you** and the implied “you” in the imperatives **Go** and **enter** are masculine singular to agree with the term **people**. It seems that when he uses a feminine form of “hide,” Isaiah is alluding to the image in verses 17 and 18 of the nation as a woman giving birth. So use the feminine form for this imperative if your language marks that distinction.

Isaiah is speaking of **fury** as if it were a living thing that could **pass by** a place. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the fury is over]

21.note: Isaiah is using **behold Yahweh, coming out** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh is about to come out.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is about to come out]
Here, **to visit the iniquity** marks punishing the earth’s inhabitants as the purpose of Yahweh **coming out from his place**. Alternate translation: [coming to earth to punish]

Here, **his place** represents heaven, where Yahweh dwells. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from his dwelling in heaven]

Isaiah is using **visit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to bring punishment on]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the evil deeds of]

Isaiah is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could **uncover** hidden blood. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the blood shed on it will be revealed]

Here, **its blood** represents the evidence of violent deaths that have occurred on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the evidence of those who were murdered on it]

Isaiah is speaking of **the earth** as if it were a living thing that could deliberately **cover over its slain** to hide them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the murdered will no longer be hidden]
